new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. First stress-bearing evidence of any kind for Abu, but it is per-word accent marking in a secondary transcription of a 1971 survey wordlist, not a statement; it does not establish a placement rule (tendency: second syllable / final in disyllables, with exceptions). Z'graggen 1969 (held by the project, read) explicitly omitted stress marking for all Madang-survey languages, so there is no other source to agree or conflict with.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated anywhere (wordlist notebook; the derivative is a comparative table). Evidence type: per-word acute accents on Laycock's Abu forms. Reader's tally over DISTINCT accented polysyllabic forms in the copy consulted (my count, not a source statement): Adjora village (Laycock) 47 forms - accent on the 2nd syllable in 32 (disyllables: final 26 vs initial 8; trisyllables: penult 6, final 4, antepenult 2; one 4-syllable penult); Gwin village (Laycock) 40 forms - 2nd syllable in 32 (disyllables: final 23 vs initial 2; trisyllables: penult 9, final 2, antepenult 2; two 4-syllable penult). Counting from the word end instead: Adjora final 30 / penult 15 / antepenult 2; Gwin final 25 / penult 13 / antepenult 2. About 60% of the Laycock Abu forms carry no accent at all (49 of 133 Adjora, 42 of 130 Gwin distinct forms are accented). So stress as Laycock heard it is not on one fixed syllable counted from either edge; the strongest tendency is second-syllable (= final in the many vowel-initial disyllables such as agún 'rain', aməní 'louse', ɔŋә́ 'village', ɔtә́m 'yam', ampә́ 'house'; penult in trisyllables such as andʒɨ́nə 'sago', ukanáme, ŋkanáma), with counter-cases (túwə, ámban, ɛ́rən, ágəre initial; əŋkəní, gʷurabɨ́r final in trisyllables). This is impressionistic survey transcription passed through two hands; it supports no catalog rule by itself.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none marked except one Adjora form gʷídʒɪnì (acute + grave) in the derivative; nothing stated
